rows.name: fifo-why
rows.question: Why does index equality alone not distinguish full from empty? Give the two concrete capacity-17 states and show how your actual implementation distinguishes them.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Why does index equality alone not distinguish full from empty? Give the two concrete capacity-17 states and show how your actual implementation distinguishes them.
rows.answer:
Index equality alone is ambiguous because the indices wrap modulo 17. In the actual implementation, these two concrete states both have head_ == tail_:

- Initially empty: head_ = 0, tail_ = 0, count_ = 0.
- After pushing values 0 through 16: head_ = 0, tail_ = 0, count_ = 17; all 17 slots are occupied.

The implementation distinguishes them using count_: empty() checks count_ == 0, while full() checks count_ == capacity. The invariant is 0 <= count_ <= 17 and tail_ == (head_ + count_) % 17; push rejects when count_ == 17, and pop rejects when count_ == 0, before changing any state.

review.note: Actual empty0/0/count0 and full0/0/count17 distinguish equal indices. Correct modulo invariant and guard-before-mutation.
review.usefulPrefix: Index equality alone is ambiguous because the indices wrap modulo 17.

rows.name: floating-counterexample
rows.question: Under IEEE binary32, round after each addition and forbid reassociation. Evaluate (16777216 + -16777216) + 1 and 16777216 + (-16777216 + 1). Then change the leftmost operand to positive 16777216, the middle operand to 1, and the last operand to -16777216. Compare both parenthesizations of that changed triple. Explain representability at each intermediate step; do not simply cite nonassociativity.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Under IEEE binary32, round after each addition and forbid reassociation. Evaluate (16777216 + -16777216) + 1 and 16777216 + (-16777216 + 1). Then change the leftmost operand to positive 16777216, the middle operand to 1, and the last operand to -16777216. Compare both parenthesizations of that changed triple. Explain representability at each intermediate step; do not simply cite nonassociativity.
rows.answer:
Assuming IEEE binary32’s default round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, the original expressions both give 1; the changed triple gives 0 with left grouping and 1 with right grouping.

Original triple:
• (16777216 + -16777216) + 1: cancellation produces exactly 0, then 0 + 1 produces exactly 1.
• 16777216 + (-16777216 + 1): the inner result is -16777215, which is exactly representable; adding 16777216 then produces exactly 1.

Changed triple:
• (16777216 + 1) + -16777216: the exact inner sum, 16777217, is not representable. At this magnitude, the adjacent binary32 values are 16777216 and 16777218. The sum is halfway between them, so ties-to-even rounds it to 16777216; the final cancellation produces 0.
• 16777216 + (1 + -16777216): the inner result is exactly representable as -16777215, and the final addition produces exactly 1.

The key boundary is 2²⁴ = 16777216: spacing immediately below it is 1, but immediately above it is 2. Thus -16777215 is representable, whereas positive 16777217 is not.

review.note: Qualifies round-to-nearest ties-even. Original both1, changed0/1, precise representability and asymmetric spacing either side of2^24, no reassociation.
review.usefulPrefix: Assuming IEEE binary32’s default round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, the original expressions both give 1; the changed triple gives 0 with left grouping and 1 with right grouping.

rows.name: quorum-counterexample
rows.question: Five replicas A,B,C,D,E retain the highest version. A writer finishes after three acknowledgements. A reader queries any three and returns the highest version, without write-back. Prove or disprove linearizability including reads overlapping an incomplete write: give a fully ordered execution with two nonoverlapping reads and show the attempted linearization contradiction. Then change only the reader to write the selected version to three replicas before returning and explain whether this fixes the counterexample.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Five replicas A,B,C,D,E retain the highest version. A writer finishes after three acknowledgements. A reader queries any three and returns the highest version, without write-back. Prove or disprove linearizability including reads overlapping an incomplete write: give a fully ordered execution with two nonoverlapping reads and show the attempted linearization contradiction. Then change only the reader to write the selected version to three replicas before returning and explain whether this fixes the counterexample.
rows.answer:
Without read write-back, this is not linearizable: a reader can expose an incomplete write, then a later reader can return the old value.

Initially, all five replicas hold version 0. Here is a fully ordered execution:
1. A writer invokes W(1). Only A stores version 1 and acknowledges; deliveries to B,C,D,E are delayed, so W remains incomplete.
2. R1 starts, queries A,B,C, receives versions 1,0,0, and returns 1.
3. After R1 returns, R2 starts, queries B,D,E, receives 0,0,0, and returns 0.
4. Only afterward, deliver W to B and C. They store 1 and acknowledge, allowing W to finish with three acknowledgements.

To explain R1 returning 1, the attempted linearization must place W before R1. Real-time order requires R1 before R2, so W must also precede R2. With no intervening write, R2 must return 1, contradicting its actual return of 0. An incomplete write may be linearized during its execution, but it cannot be placed differently for different readers.

Requiring a reader to write its selected version to three replicas and receive their acknowledgements before returning fixes this counterexample. When R1 returns 1, at least three replicas retain version 1 or higher. Every subsequent three-replica query intersects that set because 3 + 3 > 5; therefore R2 must see and return version 1 or higher, never 0.

For the general linearizability guarantee, versions must uniquely identify writes and respect the real-time order of writes—for example, a single writer using increasing sequence numbers. Under that assumption, both completed writes and completed reads leave their version or higher on a quorum, preventing later operations from going backward. Reads exposing an incomplete write can be ordered after that write, and reads selecting the same version can be ordered consistently with real time. With multiple writers, merely saying “highest version” is insufficient: a correct version-allocation protocol is also needed.

review.note: Actual pending A-only write1; R1ABC1 then R2BDE0 after R1 response; only afterward write completes. W<R1<R2 contradicts returned0. Processed quorum writeback prevents regression; general claim properly qualifies real-time ordered unique versions/single writer and multiwriter allocation.
review.usefulPrefix: Without read write-back, this is not linearizable: a reader can expose an incomplete write, then a later reader can return the old value.

rows.name: quorum-why
rows.question: Why does the second read have to respect a value returned by the first read even if the writer never completed? State the relevant real-time order and distinguish it from requiring every unfinished operation to complete.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Why does the second read have to respect a value returned by the first read even if the writer never completed? State the relevant real-time order and distinguish it from requiring every unfinished operation to complete.
rows.answer:
Because the two completed reads must fit one legal sequential register history, and the first read returns before the second is invoked: R1 < R2 in real-time order.

If R1 returns version 1, the pending W(1) must be included in the linearization before R1 to explain that value. Thus W(1) < R1 < R2, so R2 cannot return version 0 when no intervening write restores it.

This does not require every unfinished operation to complete. Linearizability allows pending operations to be omitted or supplied with a completion when constructing the history, but this particular write cannot be omitted because its value was returned by a completed read.

review.note: One legal sequential history plus R1 response before R2 invocation forces W<R1<R2. Value-returning pending write cannot be omitted; no assertion that all unfinished operations actually finish.
review.usefulPrefix: Because the two completed reads must fit one legal sequential register history, and the first read returns before the second is invoked: R1 < R2 in real-time order.

After B’s failed CAS, expected changes from 0 to 1, but desired remains 1 in the buggy code. Retrying with those values can succeed by replacing 1 with 1, so A and B both finish but the counter is only 1; recomputing desired = expected + 1 makes B store 2 instead.
